lessonTitle: The Euler Turbomachine Equation and Velocity Triangles

blocks.text: A centrifugal pump at 1450 rev/min lifts water from a sump to a header tank 30 m above, yet nothing inside it is mysterious: the impeller simply throws the water outward and spins it up. How much pressure head it adds is fixed by only two things, how fast the blade tips move and how much swirl the fluid has on leaving. That relationship is the Euler turbomachine equation.

blocks.markdown: A **turbomachine** exchanges energy between a rotating element (the impeller or runner) and a continuously flowing fluid. Pumps and compressors add energy to the fluid; turbines remove it. The simplest route to the work transfer uses **angular momentum**. In steady flow the torque exerted on the fluid by the impeller equals the net rate at which angular momentum leaves the control volume, which depends only on conditions at the inlet (1) and outlet (2). No knowledge of the detailed flow path between them is needed.

blocks.caption: Euler turbomachine equation: torque, power and specific work (J/kg)

blocks.title: Symbols and velocity triangles
blocks.text: $r$ is radius (m), $\omega$ angular speed (rad/s), $u=\omega r$ blade speed (m/s), $c$ absolute velocity of the fluid, $c_\theta$ its tangential (swirl) component, $c_m$ the meridional (radial through-flow) component and $\dot m=\rho Q$ the mass flow (kg/s). The fluid velocity relative to the blade is $w_r$. At every station the three vectors form the **velocity triangle**: $\mathbf c=\mathbf u+\mathbf w_r$.

blocks.markdown: For a pump the ideal (loss-free) **head** $H$ (m of fluid) is the specific work divided by gravity, $H=w/g$. Many pumps draw their flow axially or radially without pre-rotation, so $c_{\theta1}=0$ and the equation simplifies to $H=u_2c_{\theta2}/g$. To find $c_{\theta2}$ we use the outlet triangle. For a blade whose tip makes the angle $\beta_2$ with the tangent (measured so that $\beta_2<90^\circ$ means **backward-curved**), the relative velocity has component $c_{m2}$ normal to the tangent, so $c_{\theta2}=u_2-c_{m2}/\tan\beta_2$, where $c_{m2}=Q/(\pi D_2b_2)$ for an impeller of outlet diameter $D_2$ and outlet width $b_2$.

blocks.caption: Ideal pump head for radial inlet (N in rev/min); slip and losses neglected

blocks.title: Ideal head of a pump impeller
blocks.prompt: A centrifugal pump runs at N = 1450 rev/min with outlet diameter D2 = 0.300 m, outlet width b2 = 20.0 mm and outlet blade angle beta2 = 25 degrees. It delivers Q = 0.040 m^3/s of water (density 998 kg/m^3) with radial entry. Neglect slip and losses and find the ideal head and the power transferred to the water.

steps.text: Blade speed at the outlet tip from the rotational speed.
Meridional velocity at the outlet from continuity through the cylindrical area pi D2 b2.
Outlet triangle: swirl component = blade speed minus the part carried by the backward relative flow.
Specific work and head from the Euler equation with c_theta1 = 0.
Power transferred to the fluid is mass flow times specific work (mass flow = 998 x 0.040 = 39.92 kg/s).

blocks.answer: u2 = 22.78 m/s, c_theta2 = 18.23 m/s, ideal H = 42.3 m, P = 16.6 kW.

blocks.title: Inlet velocity triangle for the same pump
blocks.prompt: The same pump has an inlet (eye) diameter D1 = 0.150 m and inlet width b1 = 30.0 mm and the flow enters without swirl at Q = 0.040 m^3/s and N = 1450 rev/min. Find the blade speed, the inlet meridional velocity and the inlet blade angle for shock-free entry.

steps.text: Blade speed at the inlet eye from the rotational speed and diameter.
Meridional velocity at the inlet; with no swirl the absolute velocity c1 is purely radial and equals c_m1.
The inlet triangle is right-angled: the relative velocity has the radial component c_m1 and a tangential component u1 opposite the blade motion.
Hence the blade angle at the inlet that gives shock-free entry.

blocks.answer: u1 = 11.39 m/s, c_m1 = 2.83 m/s and beta1 = 14.0 degrees.

rows: Most common in pumps; stable, efficient
Much of the head is kinetic; unstable, used in small fans
blocks.caption: Effect of outlet blade angle on ideal work (loss-free, no slip)

items: Choose the control volume: inlet (1) and outlet (2) of the impeller.
Compute the blade speeds $u_1=\pi D_1N/60$ and $u_2=\pi D_2N/60$ (N in rev/min).
Use the velocity triangles to obtain the swirl components $c_{\theta1}$ and $c_{\theta2}$.
Apply $w=u_2c_{\theta2}-u_1c_{\theta1}$ and $H=w/g$; power is $\dot m w$.

blocks.title: Euler head is an upper limit
blocks.text: The Euler equation gives the energy transferred to the fluid by the impeller assuming the fluid follows the blades exactly. Real pumps develop less head because of blade slip (the fluid lags the blades), friction and shock losses. The ideal head is therefore the starting point for the real head-flow curve.

blocks.title: Mind the sign conventions
blocks.text: Use the angle convention in the problem: some books measure $\beta$ from the tangent, others from the radial direction. If $\beta_2$ is quoted from the radial direction, use $c_{\theta2}=u_2-c_{m2}\tan\beta_2$ instead. Always sketch the triangle first.

points: The Euler equation $w=u_2c_{\theta2}-u_1c_{\theta1}$ follows from the angular momentum balance and depends only on the inlet and outlet velocity triangles.
Pump head is $H=(u_2c_{\theta2}-u_1c_{\theta1})/g$, reducing to $u_2c_{\theta2}/g$ for radial entry.
The outlet triangle gives $c_{\theta2}=u_2-c_{m2}/\tan\beta_2$, with $c_{m2}=Q/(\pi D_2b_2)$.
Ideal head grows as the square of blade speed, so it rises strongly with impeller diameter and speed.

questions.stem: Which expression gives the specific work (J/kg) done on the fluid by an impeller with inlet 1 and outlet 2, according to the Euler turbomachine equation?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this comes from the rate of change of angular momentum.
distractorRationale.b: This is only the kinetic energy increase, not the total work.
distractorRationale.c: This is the pressure rise alone; some work appears as kinetic energy as well, and losses mean it is not the same as w.
distractorRationale.d: The meridional components carry no angular momentum about the axis, so they do not appear.

questions.explanation: The torque on the fluid equals $\dot m(r_2c_{\theta2}-r_1c_{\theta1})$ and the power is torque times $\omega$; dividing by $\dot m$ gives $w=u_2c_{\theta2}-u_1c_{\theta1}$. Only the tangential velocity components carry angular momentum about the axis.

questions.stem: To apply the Euler turbomachine equation you need to know the detailed path of the fluid inside the impeller passages between inlet and outlet.
questions.explanation: The angular momentum balance for a control volume depends only on the velocity components at the inlet and outlet surfaces, not on what happens between them. The complicated internal flow affects losses but not the ideal work.

questions.stem: A centrifugal pump impeller has an outlet diameter of 0.25 m and turns at 1750 rev/min. Water enters without swirl and leaves with a tangential velocity component of 9.5 m/s. Taking g = 9.81 m/s^2 and neglecting losses, find the ideal head in metres.
questions.explanation: The blade tip speed is u2 = pi(0.25)(1750)/60 = 22.91 m/s. With radial entry, H = u2 c_theta2/g = 22.91 x 9.5/9.81 = 22.18 m.

questions.stem: At the outlet of a pump impeller the blade tip speed is 18.0 m/s, the meridional velocity is 2.4 m/s and the blades are backward-curved with outlet angle 30 degrees measured from the tangent. Find the tangential component of the absolute velocity, c_theta2, in m/s, using the outlet velocity triangle and ignoring slip.
questions.explanation: The relative velocity has tangential component c_m2/tan(30) = 2.4/0.5774 = 4.157 m/s against the blade motion. Thus c_theta2 = 18.0 - 4.157 = 13.84 m/s.

questions.stem: For the same blade tip speed and same meridional velocity, how does the ideal (Euler) head of an impeller with forward-curved blades (outlet angle above 90 degrees) compare with that of backward-curved blades?

options.text: It is smaller, because the relative velocity is larger
It is zero, because forward-curved blades cannot transfer work
It is the same, because the head depends only on tip speed
It is larger, because the swirl component c_theta2 is larger

questions.correctOptionText: It is larger, because the swirl component c_theta2 is larger

distractorRationale.a: The relative velocity is not what appears in the Euler head; the swirl is.
distractorRationale.b: Forward-curved blades transfer the most ideal work but with poor diffusion efficiency.
distractorRationale.c: Head depends on c_theta2 as well as u2, and c_theta2 changes with blade angle.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: with beta2 > 90 degrees, tan is negative and c_theta2 exceeds u2.

questions.explanation: Since $H=u_2c_{\theta2}/g$ and $c_{\theta2}=u_2-c_{m2}/\tan\beta_2$, a forward-curved blade ($\tan\beta_2<0$) gives $c_{\theta2}>u_2$ and hence the greatest ideal head. In practice much of this is kinetic energy that is hard to convert to pressure, so efficiency suffers.

questions.stem: A pump with radial inlet delivers 0.025 m^3/s of water (density 998 kg/m^3) and develops an ideal (Euler) head of 18.0 m. Taking g = 9.81 m/s^2, find the power transferred to the water by the impeller in watts.
questions.explanation: The specific work is w = gH = 9.81 x 18.0 = 176.6 J/kg and the mass flow is 998 x 0.025 = 24.95 kg/s. Power = mass flow x w = 24.95 x 176.6 = 4406 W.

questions.stem: Water enters an impeller with no pre-swirl (radial entry). What does this say about the Euler equation for this machine?

distractorRationale.a: The blade speed at the inlet is omega r1, nonzero; the product u1 c_theta1 is zero because c_theta1 is zero.
distractorRationale.b: The outlet is where swirl is imparted; it is nonzero.
distractorRationale.c: With radial entry the velocity is purely meridional, which is nonzero.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the inlet angular momentum term vanishes.

questions.explanation: Zero pre-swirl means the fluid has no tangential velocity at the inlet, so $c_{\theta1}=0$ and the inlet term $u_1c_{\theta1}$ drops out, leaving $w=u_2c_{\theta2}$. The inlet absolute velocity is purely meridional.

questions.stem: A geometrically similar impeller with 1.2 times the outlet diameter is run at the same rotational speed with similar velocity triangles. By what factor does the ideal head change?

distractorRationale.a: No basis: the factor would be 2 only if D2 doubled with H proportional to D2.
distractorRationale.b: This is the factor 1.2^3, appropriate to power-type scalings, not head.
distractorRationale.c: This assumes head is proportional to diameter, but both u2 and c_theta2 scale with D2.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: H is proportional to u2^2 which is proportional to D2^2, and 1.2^2 = 1.44.

questions.explanation: With similar triangles both $u_2$ and $c_{\theta2}$ scale with $D_2$ at fixed rotational speed, so $H=u_2c_{\theta2}/g\propto D_2^2$. A factor of 1.2 in diameter therefore gives $1.2^2=1.44$ in head.

questions.stem: Using the angular momentum principle for a steady control volume enclosing an impeller, derive the Euler turbomachine equation for the specific work. State the assumptions made, and write it for a pump with radial entry.
markingGuide: Control volume around the impeller with uniform inlet and outlet conditions; steady flow
Torque on fluid = rate of change of angular momentum: T = mdot (r2 c_theta2 - r1 c_theta1)
Power = T omega and u = omega r gives P = mdot (u2 c_theta2 - u1 c_theta1)
Specific work w = P/mdot = u2 c_theta2 - u1 c_theta1
For radial entry c_theta1 = 0, so w = u2 c_theta2 and head H = u2 c_theta2/g (ideal)
questions.explanation: Only fluid crossing the inlet and outlet surfaces carries angular momentum in or out, so the torque of the impeller on the fluid is $\dot m(r_2c_{\theta2}-r_1c_{\theta1})$. Multiplying by $\omega$ and dividing by $\dot m$ gives $w=u_2c_{\theta2}-u_1c_{\theta1}$, and with no pre-swirl $H=u_2c_{\theta2}/g$.

questions.stem: A centrifugal pump impeller turns at 960 rev/min. It has outlet diameter 0.42 m, outlet width 25 mm and outlet blade angle 22.5 degrees from the tangent, and it handles 0.080 m^3/s of water with radial entry. (a) Sketch and describe the outlet velocity triangle. (b) Calculate u2, c_m2, c_theta2 and the ideal head (neglect slip; g = 9.81 m/s^2).
markingGuide: Sketch: u2 along the tangent, relative velocity w2 at 22.5 degrees to the tangent pointing backwards, c_m2 radial, absolute velocity c2 closing the triangle
questions.explanation: The tip speed is 21.11 m/s and the radial velocity is 2.43 m/s, so the tangential relative component is 5.85 m/s and c_theta2 = 15.26 m/s. With radial entry, H = u2 c_theta2/g = 32.8 m.
